# LaCode

> Ultimate opencode setup for Go users

> LaCode 1.2.0 ships on the npm **`latest`** dist-tag. Prereleases use
> `beta`: install `@lawaty/lacode@beta`, or pin an exact version.

LaCode is an opencode plugin. It routes delegated work onto a weighted pool of
cheap models instead of the expensive one, reaps subagents that hang without
telling anyone, keeps a maintained map of your repository so agents stop
exploring it cold on every task, and tells you when a parallel session finishes
or is waiting on you — including sessions running on remote hosts over SSH,
where the desktop notification would otherwise die on a machine that has no
desktop.

Install it with one config line. It adds agents and commands it finds missing,
and it never overwrites one you already defined.

Upgrading? See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) — it ships with the package, so it
is also on disk at `node_modules/@lawaty/lacode/CHANGELOG.md`.

## Why

| Capability | The problem it solves |
| --- | --- |
| Weighted model pool | An expensive main model burns through its quota doing file listing. |
| Per-model cooldowns and failover | A provider rate-limits mid-session and the whole thing hard-fails, while other providers sit idle. |
| Hang reaper | A wedged subagent holds its slot forever, so the session stalls with no error and no timeout. |
| Desktop notifications | With several sessions open you cannot see which one finished, or which is blocked on a question. |
| Permission answers on the popup | An approval blocks a background session, and finding that session just to click Allow is the interruption. |
| Distinct notification sounds | A popup says something happened, but not at a glance whether it is a finish, a question or a block. |
| SSH notification tunnel | Work on a remote host raises its notification on that host, which has no desktop. |
| Repository context map | Every task starts by exploring your codebase cold, re-deriving the same layout, entry points and boundaries. |
| Standing instructions | The same direction gets repeated every session, or buried in config that is not per-clone. |
| Image attachments anywhere | A TUI with no image support locks vision models out entirely. |

## Getting started

### 1. Install

Add one line to your opencode config — `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`, or
the `.jsonc` beside it:

```json
{ "plugin": ["@lawaty/lacode"] }
```

**That is the entire install.** opencode resolves an npm plugin specifier itself
and installs it at startup, so there is no `npm install` to run first and no
directory to create. Do not run `npm i -g @lawaty/lacode`: a global npm install is
never consulted by opencode, so it changes nothing about whether the plugin
loads.

To install it for every project on the machine rather than per config, let the
CLI do the same thing:

```bash
opencode plugin @lawaty/lacode -g
```

### 2. Restart opencode

**Plugin code is not hot-reloaded.** The `plugin` array is read at startup, so
without a restart the change does not take effect and the agent set will look
stale for no visible reason. (The pool's slot files are the exception: editing
`pool.txt`, `pool.json` or the bundled preset is picked up live — see
[Configure](#configure).)

### 3. Check it loaded

```bash
opencode agent list | grep -E '^(explore|implement|context)'
```

You should see `explore`, `implement` and `context`, each with hidden `-1`..`-4`
pool variants alongside. That is the whole install, and you are done.

Each pool slot controls the rate-limit-reset desktop notice: it is on by
default for `opencode` and `opencode-go` slots, and other providers need
`notify:on` in `pool.txt` or `"notify": true` in `pool.json` to opt in.

**If that prints nothing, the plugin did not load** — and opencode will not tell
you: it starts normally, logs nothing, and the agents are simply absent. A
plugin that fails to load is silent by design of the host, so this check is the
only way to know. The
[troubleshooting guide](docs/INSTALL.md#if-the-agents-are-missing) walks the
procedure.

### 4. Use it

Nothing to turn on. Ask for something that delegates, and the pool takes it from
there:

```
> use the explore agent to find where auth tokens are validated
```

To see what the pool is doing underneath:

```bash
/lacode-doctor        # slots, model resolution, OmniRoute — report only, changes nothing
/pool-recheck         # probe the benched models now; re-admit the ones that answer
lacode version        # which LaCode is actually running, and whether opencode loads that one
```

In a repository with no `.opencode/context/` yet, the first session builds it in
the background; `/context-init` forces it, and [Context map](#context-map)
explains what it is for.

## Feedback

The feedback path has no telemetry and no analytics — it sends nothing anywhere
— but I would still like to hear from you.

- **Bug or feature request?** [Open an issue](https://github.com/lawaty/lacode/issues).
- **Question, or want to say how you use it?** [Start a discussion](https://github.com/lawaty/lacode/discussions).
- **Found it useful?** A ⭐ on [the repo](https://github.com/lawaty/lacode) helps
  other people find it.

`lacode feedback` prints both links. The one-time hint that points at the issue
tracker is opt-out: set `feedbackHint: false` in the plugin options, or
`LACODE_NO_FEEDBACK_HINT=1` in the environment. It is shown at most once, only
when there is a TUI to show it in; piped, CI and test runs leave the flag
untouched. A toast that fails does not consume the note, so a later interactive
run can still show it.

## Configure

Plugin options are a tuple — the package name, then an options object. Every
option is optional:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    ["@lawaty/lacode", {
      "enabled": true,
      "models": {
        "slots": [
          { "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5", "weight": 2 },
          { "model": "opencode/big-pickle", "weight": 1 }
        ]
      }
    }]
  ]
}
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | The single off switch. `false` injects nothing at all and does no writes. |
| `models` | — | An inline slot list; `weight` is that line's budget and cap, a model may repeat, and there is no slot cap. Highest-priority source. |
| `modelsFile` | — | An explicit slot file; short-circuits the [resolution chain](docs/CONFIGURATION.md#pool-preset-resolution). |
| `reapMs` | `30000` | Hang-reaper interval. |
| `probeMs` | `900000` | How often benched models are checked by actually using them. `0` turns the periodic check off and leaves the `pool_recheck` tool as the only way to ask. |
| `selfUpdate` | `true` | Check for a newer release at most once per ~6h and install it in the background; it applies on the next opencode start. `false` — or `LACODE_NO_SELFUPDATE=1` — turns the check off. |
| `feedbackHint` | `true` | Show the one-time feedback note on the first interactive run. `false` — or `LACODE_NO_FEEDBACK_HINT=1` — turns it off. The flag lives in `~/.local/share/opencode/lacode/feedback.json`; nothing is sent anywhere. |
| `sound` | `true` | Play a short tone with each notification, one per outcome, so you can tell a finished session from a question or a permission prompt without reading the popup. It is opt-out: `false` — or `LACODE_SOUND=0` (`false`, `off`, `no` work too, and beat the option) — turns the sound off, and anything else, a typo included, leaves it on. |
| `omniroute` | — | Optional [OmniRoute](docs/OMNIROUTE.md) gateway integration. Absent or `{ enabled: false }` changes nothing. |
| `yolo` | `false` | YOLO mode: permission requests that would ask are auto-approved. Explicit `deny` rules still win. The TUI writes this option when you run `/yolo`. |
| `ykb` | `false` | YKB (You Know Better) mode: the agent is told not to ask, and questions that still appear are answered with the recommended option. The TUI writes this option when you run `/ykb`. |
| `watchMs` | `1000` | How often the pool files are checked for changes. `0` disables live reload. |
| `watchDebounceMs` | `250` | Collapse a burst of editor writes into one reload. |
| `imagePaste` | — | Image attachments: `maxBytes` (4 MiB), `maxImages` (10) and `dir`. |

## Modes

Two runtime modes live on the lacode plugin entry and can be toggled from the TUI:

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `/yolo` | Toggle YOLO. Every permission request that would `ask` is approved automatically; an explicit `deny` still wins. |
| `/ykb` | Toggle YKB (You Know Better). The agent is told not to ask questions and to continue with its recommendation. A question that still appears is answered with its `(Recommended)` option, or its first option when none is marked. |
| `/modes` | Show both switches. |

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    ["@lawaty/lacode", { "yolo": true, "ykb": false }]
  ]
}
```

The toggles edit the `yolo` / `ykb` options on the lacode plugin entry in your global opencode config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/opencode.jsonc`), preserving comments. The server reads that file on the next decision — no restart. Turning a mode on also answers requests that are already pending. The lacode plugin entry must already exist in the global config; a project-only entry cannot be toggled. A free-text question with no options is left for the user, since there is no option to choose.

### Staying up to date

opencode's plugin cache is **write-once**: it resolves `@lawaty/lacode` to an
exact version once and never re-resolves — not on restart, not with
`opencode plugin -g -f`, not with a range pin, not with a tagged config spec.
Nothing in the host re-resolves it, so the plugin owns its own currency
(US-27): at startup LaCode compares its own version to npm's `latest` (at most
once per ~6h, silent when offline) and, when behind, reinstalls its own cache
entry in the background using the opencode binary — no npm or bun required.
The running session keeps its loaded code; the new version takes effect on the
next start, and the log says so. Run `lacode update` to do it on demand, or
`lacode update --check` to just report.

1.2.0 is published to the `latest` dist-tag; prereleases use `beta`. This check
follows `latest`. A beta install is therefore reported as current even when a
newer beta exists,
and `lacode update` will not move it: pin the version you want in the `plugin`
entry, because a new specifier is what forces a fresh resolve.

### Which LaCode is running

`lacode version` answers it — and the answer is often not the version number you
expected, because the plugin entry in your config decides which copy is loaded:

```bash
lacode version
```

```
version    1.2.0
root       /home/you/lacode
source     checkout
commit     <hash> (dirty)
dist       current
config     /home/you/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc
plugin     file:///home/you/lacode/dist/index.js
this copy  yes — opencode loads this copy
```

`npm ls -g @lawaty/lacode` answers a different question. It reports the package
opencode resolves *by name*, which is not necessarily the one running: a config
may load the plugin by absolute path, and a global install can sit there
reporting a version nothing uses. So this command reads your actual `plugin`
array and says whether it resolves to the copy speaking.

`source` distinguishes a git checkout from an npm install, `commit` and the
dirty flag name what the code was built from, and `dist` is the trap worth
knowing about — opencode loads `dist/index.js` while you edit and pull `src/`,
so a `git pull` can leave you running a build that differs from the installed
package, with nothing failing.
When it reports `stale`, rebuild with `npm run build`. No network is touched;
`lacode update --check` is what asks npm whether something newer exists.

## What you get

Three pooled agents: `explore`, `implement` and `context`. You spawn the base
name and the pool picks a cheap model slot for it. Behind each base sits one
hidden variant per slot — however many the pool declares — and a spawn of the
bare name is the only thing that works: a hand-named variant such as `explore-1`
is coerced to its base and routed by the pool, so naming one cannot pin a
provider or skip ordered slot filling.

A slot's `weight` is both its concurrency budget and its cap: the pool fills
slots in declaration order in one pass, then overflows to the least-loaded slot.
There is no slot cap, and a model may appear on more than one line — each line
is a separate slot with its own weight — so to give a model more capacity, list
it again.

A model that rate-limits or runs out of quota is benched until its window ends,
so one sick provider does not take the pool with it.
Those windows are computed backoff rather than a promise from the provider,
and a quota-shaped one can run for hours — long enough for a provider that has
since recovered, or whose quota you reset in its own console, to stay excluded
while every delegated spawn queues behind the survivors. So LaCode asks instead
of guessing: every fifteen minutes, on demand via the `pool_recheck` tool, and
the moment a pool file changes (where it validates every slot, cooling or not),
it probes each benched model with one real request on that exact model. A model
that answers is re-admitted immediately — nothing restarts, nothing reloads — and
a model that is still limited keeps exactly the window it had, because a check
must never be the thing that extends the wait. A model the provider does not
serve at all is benched for the quota cap and named in the report.
A change is reported as a toast and a log line; a pass that finds nothing changed says
nothing at all.

Ten commands: `/context-init`, `/context-update`, `/context-review`,
`/lacode-doctor`, `/agent-instructions`, `/pool`, `/pool-recheck`,
`/reprocess-timeline`, `/image-in-cb` and `/image`. Everything is added **only when your config does not already
define it** — an agent or command you wrote yourself is left byte-identical,
never patched or partially merged. `{"enabled": false}` turns the whole thing off
without leaving a trace. The exact injection list, and the five keys that are
deliberately *not* injected, are in
[docs/CONFIGURATION.md](docs/CONFIGURATION.md#what-gets-injected).

Two more surfaces that need no configuration:

- **`pool_status`** — the live view `/lacode-doctor` uses: per-slot load against
  its ceiling, which slot the next spawn takes, cooldowns, hung claims and
  whether the watcher is on. Ask for it when you want to know what the pool is
  doing; it never changes slot selection.
- **Notifications that wait** — a notification is never auto-dismissed; it stays
  until you close it. On Linux a permission request carries **Allow once**,
  **Always allow** and **Deny** buttons, and LaCode waits up to ten minutes for
  the click.

## Context map

Agents are stateless between tasks, and exploring your repository is the most
expensive part of any task — so every agent pays for it again, re-deriving the
same layout, entry points and boundaries from scratch. LaCode keeps a short,
maintained map of the repository in `.opencode/context/` — five navigation files
(`architecture`, `contexts`, `conventions`, `workflows`, `decisions`) — and injects
a standing rule that every agent reads the relevant file before exploring and
starts from the canonical entry points it lists. The map holds conclusions, not
inventories: it answers "what should I look at first?" and nothing else, which
is what makes reading it cheaper than the exploration it replaces.

It keeps itself current. When a session that edited code goes idle, LaCode
starts a `context` run that borrows a slot from the same pool every
other subagent uses and updates the map from the changed paths and their
architectural neighbourhood — defaulting to *no edit*, since a changed file is
not a changed fact. Only that one agent ever writes the map; everything else
reports what belongs in it, so concurrent sessions cannot contradict each other.
You can also drive it by hand, which is the move when you do not trust what you
are reading:

```bash
/context-init      # build the map, or verify and refresh an existing one
/context-update    # incremental refresh; accepts a focus, e.g. /context-update src/payments
/context-review    # audit it for staleness, contradictions, duplication and bloat
/lacode-doctor     # check the pool, model resolution and the OmniRoute gateway. Report only
/agent-instructions # apply a client instruction to the project's AGENTS.md — client-only, see below
/pool              # rewrite the pool slot table in ~/.config/lacode/pool.txt; picked up automatically
/pool-recheck      # probe the pool now; accepts an optional provider/model list
/image-in-cb       # attach the clipboard image to this message; macOS needs pngpaste, Linux needs wl-paste or xclip
/image             # attach one or more image files to this message; paths honour quotes, ~ and globs
```

The map is local and untracked — it describes your checkout on your machine, so
it is not committed and not synced. If it is missing, agents check, find
nothing and carry on without it. What this buys is tokens not spent
re-discovering structure; as with everything else here, no savings percentage is
published, because none has been independently measured. The mechanism, the
permission rule that makes one writer possible, and what the log lines mean are
in [docs/CONTEXT.md](docs/CONTEXT.md). Automatic map runs also clean up after
themselves: each run's session is deleted once its transcript is written, and
the last 20 transcripts are kept under
`~/.local/share/opencode/lacode/cartographer` (`LACODE_TRANSCRIPT_DIR` overrides
the directory).

## Standing instructions

The project's root `AGENTS.md` — created on first use by `/agent-instructions` —
is your own statement of intent: it records
what you want worked on and how you want it approached. It says nothing about
where code lives, so it can never contradict the code, and within that domain
it outranks the generated context files and any agent's inference about what
matters right now.

The file is per-clone and not committed, so it is yours rather than shared
team state. There is no fixed schema and no prescribed headings — you write
whatever you like, and every heading you add is treated as direction.

Anything you have recorded there is read before work starts, and what you have
recorded is treated as settled by the agents — not as permission to skip
reading the code.

**Who may write it.** Every agent is explicitly permission-denied from
touching this path, so no automatic run can ever alter it. The one exception
is the hidden `instructions` agent, reachable solely through the
`/agent-instructions` command.

**`/agent-instructions` — the one sanctioned write path.** Type
`/agent-instructions <text>` and the `instructions` agent applies whatever
instruction you have given to `AGENTS.md`, then reports what it changed. It is
a normal agent turn, not a dead append: tell it what you want and review the
result. The `instructions` agent is the one agent permitted to edit that file,
its write grant is scoped to `AGENTS.md` alone, and no other agent can spawn it —
the command is the only route in. It may also **read** `.opencode/context/`, so a
directive does not restate a fact the map has already settled or contradict one it
has not read; the map stays read-only to it, and the `context` agent remains its
only writer.

## Cost

The mechanism is specific and small: bulk exploration, implementation and
repository cartography run on pooled cheap or free subagents instead of the main
model. There are **two separate effects** here, and they are worth telling apart
because only one of them is about money per token:

1. **The tokens are spent on a cheaper model.** A read, a grep, or a mechanical
   edit performed by a near-free subagent costs per-token approximately nothing,
   where the same call on your main model does not. This is the effect people
   usually mean when they say the pool saves money.
2. **The main model's context is never filled with file contents it does not
   need.** A delegated explorer returns a conclusion and a `file:line`, not
   forty tool calls' worth of source. The expensive model spends its attention
   on design work instead of on reconstructing a directory tree, and its context
   window — a hard, non-renewable budget — is spent on reasoning rather than on
   raw file text.

The second is the larger of the two, and it is not a cost-per-token effect at
all: it is a capacity effect. It holds even when the pooled model is not free,
and it is why the pool is scoped to *mechanical* work. Work that needs real
judgement belongs to the main model regardless of what the pool is running,
because pulling a difficult conclusion back through a subagent costs more
context on the far side than reading the file directly would have.

That scoping is why the bundled preset is free: pooled work is work you would
not have wanted the main model to do anyway. **Free is the shipped default, not
an enforced restriction.** The pool is open — it accepts any model you give it,
free, cheap or expensive, and never inspects, prices, warns about, filters or
rewrites one. The only per-model rule is structural: a slot must be written
`provider/model-id` so it is addressable at all. That default lives in exactly one
place, `presets/free-tier.json`, where you can read it and change it (US-7, US-23).

Agents start from the maintained context map above rather than exploring cold, so
the structure of your codebase is written down once instead of re-derived on
every task. Load is counted per model across every agent type and every process,
so a slot cannot hide behind its own dedicated model while another idles, and a
model that just rate-limited one project is skipped by all of them.

**No savings percentage is published here, because none has been independently
measured.** What the mechanism is worth in money depends entirely on the token
mix of your tasks and on the models you compare the pooled run against. A figure
from someone else's workload is not a claim about yours.

The harness exists so you can produce your own number:

```bash
npm run benchmark          # offline simulation from the pinned price snapshot
npm run benchmark -- --real   # runs both sides for real and reads back the tokens
```

Both print tokens and cost for the same scenario run two ways, and both refuse
to emit a number they cannot derive — an unpriced model reports `unknown`, never
`0`. How the two modes differ is in [docs/BENCHMARKS.md](docs/BENCHMARKS.md),
which explains the harness and deliberately contains no results.

`npm run score` is the other measurement: it probes each configured provider's
free models with one tiny request and ranks them by measured latency, context and
output limit. It prints a suggested `pool.txt` but never edits it, and writes the
raw rows to `~/.config/lacode/model-scores.json`. Run it every few days — free
models and quota windows move.

## Remote hosts

Notifications raised on a remote host need a way back to your desktop. The
default hop is a direct `ssh` to your desktop over one warm `ControlMaster`
connection; a reverse forward is the fallback used when `OC_LOCAL_HOST` is unset:

```bash
lacode notify "build finished" "4 files changed"      # local desktop, or forwarded if remote
lacode doctor                                        # what the environment resolves to
```

`lacode notify` is fire-and-forget and always exits 0 — an unreachable desktop
must never be able to fail the process that tried to notify you. The one
exception is an actionable notification — one carrying a permission request id
— which waits for the click, because the answer is the whole point of it.
That click path is Linux-only: the popup carries **Allow once**, **Always allow**
and **Deny**, and macOS gets a plain notice without buttons.
`lacode forward HOST -- COMMAND` runs a command on another host over ssh and
exits with its status.

The full CLI is `notify`, `forward`, `doctor`, `feedback`, `version`, `update`,
`receive` and `tunnel setup`. `version` reports which copy of LaCode is running —
and whether opencode is loading that same copy — and `update [--check]` refreshes
an installed one. `feedback` prints the Issues and Discussions links; it opens
nothing and sends nothing. `receive` is the desktop end of the tunnel (the forced
command a remote key is restricted to) and `tunnel setup` provisions the key and
the forward.

Configuration, the payload format, the receiver contract and holding the forward
open are in [docs/TUNNEL.md](docs/TUNNEL.md).

## Development

```bash
npm run build          # esbuild -> dist/ (what the tarball ships)
npm test               # node --test tests/ — offline, no network, no running server
npm run benchmark      # the cost harness; see docs/BENCHMARKS.md
npm run score          # rank free models by context, output and measured latency
```

Node ≥ 22.18.

`npm run build` compiles each entry point in `package.json` (`exports` and
`bin`) into `dist/` with esbuild, one bundle per entry point, so nothing in
`src/` has to be renamed to satisfy node's ESM resolver. `@opencode-ai/plugin`
and the node builtins are external — see the header of `scripts/build.mjs` for
why a peer dependency must never be inlined. `dist/` is generated and
gitignored; `prepack` builds it, so `npm pack` cannot produce a stale tarball.

The sources are TypeScript and the tests import `src/` directly (node strips the
types outside `node_modules`, which is exactly where the tests live), so the
loop is: edit `src/`, run `npm test`. Only the packaging fixtures build, and
they call the same `scripts/build.mjs` the tarball does.

`tests/stories/` holds the story suites and `tests/stories/coverage.test.mjs`
is the guard: it reads the `### US-N:` headings out of `docs/USER-STORIES.md`
and the `[US-N]` markers out of the test names and fails if they disagree, in
either direction. **A test that covers a story must have the id at the start of
its name** — `test("[US-7] a paid model is accepted")` — or the coverage guard
fails it.
A story with no test is as much a failure as a test naming a story that does not
exist.

# Pool presets

A preset is the pool's slot list: which models your pooled subagents share, and
how many concurrent sessions each one gets. It is one JSON file.

## Resolution chain

LaCode reads the first source that yields usable slots, in this order:

| # | Source | Where |
|---|--------|-------|
| 1 | plugin options | `["@lawaty/lacode", { "models": { "slots": [...] } }]` |
| 2 | user config | `~/.config/lacode/pool.txt` (flat, preferred) or `~/.config/lacode/pool.json` (JSON) |
| 3 | bundled preset | `presets/free-tier.json` |
| 4 | built-in fallback | hardcoded in `src/lib/pool.ts`, so routing always works |

The same logic lives in `resolveModels()` in `src/lib/pool.ts`, and it is the
single place it is implemented.

Missing, unreadable, or structurally broken falls **through to the next link**
and logs one warning. Nothing here ever throws into opencode — a pool that cannot
route takes every parallel spawn in the process down with it. Source 2's parent
directory (`~/.config/lacode/`) is created at plugin startup so you can drop a
file in without `mkdir` first.

Sources 1 and 2 win outright: if they parse, the bundled preset is never read.
Source 3 is a default, not a floor.

The pool files are not frozen at startup: the running process watches them,
reloads the slot table, re-binds the variant agents and validates every slot, so a
change here takes effect without a restart. Plugin CODE still needs one.

## The flat pool file (recommended)

`~/.config/lacode/pool.txt` is one model per line — edit a model id or a weight
in place, no JSON and no objects:

```text
# provider/model-id                       weight  c:<context>
opencode/big-pickle                       3       c:200000
opencode-go/beam-free       2       c:200000
opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free         1       c:200000
opencode/glm-5.3-flash-free               1       c:200000
```

`#` starts a comment (whole-line or trailing), blank lines are ignored, and the
weight is optional (default 1). `c:<context>` is the model's context window in tokens; the router uses it to prefer the smallest model that fits the task, and it is optional for hand-written lines. The rules are exactly the same as the JSON form
below: any number of slots, a model may repeat on another line, split on the
first slash only. The loader accepts either shape in the same file, so a leading
`{` means JSON and anything else means the flat form.

## Schema

```jsonc
{
  "slots": [
    { "model": "provider/model-id", "weight": 3 },
    { "model": "provider/another-id" }        // weight defaults to 1
  ]
}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|-------|----------|---------|
| `model` | yes | `provider/model-id`, split on the **first** slash only |
| `weight` | no | active-session budget; the pool's capacity is the sum of the weights. Absent = 1 |

`$comment` is a JSON-legal array of strings and is ignored by the loader; the
bundled preset uses it to explain itself in place.

## Validation — structure only

The loader checks shape and nothing else:

- `slots` must be a non-empty array
- each `model` must contain a `/`
- a model may appear on more than one line; each line is its own slot with its
  own load counter and weight
- `weight` must be a number in `(0, 100]`; a bad one **warns and uses 1** rather
  than dropping the slot, because losing a model to a typo in a count costs real
  capacity
- there is no slot cap: one hidden variant agent is declared per base per
  resolved slot, and the watcher declares a variant if a reload grows the table
- `tier` is accepted as an alias for `weight` (`primary` → 2,
  `overflow` → 1) and warns

**Cost is never validated.** Any provider/model-id string is accepted, including
paid and proprietary models. There is no free-tier allowlist anywhere in the
package — a preset of frontier models is exactly as valid as the bundled one. The
bundled preset is built from 0/0-cost models because that is a good default, not
because the pool requires it.

## Weight, precisely

A weight is a slot's active-session budget: the number of concurrent claims it
may hold before the next slot is preferred. The pool's capacity is the **sum of
the weights**, so a weight-3 slot may hold 3 concurrent sessions and listing a
model on two lines gives it two independent budgets.

Routing is one pass:

1. fill each usable slot up to its weight, in declaration order

A slot is skipped when it is cooling or unavailable. When every usable slot is
at its weight, the pool is at capacity and overflow goes to the least loaded
usable slot; the pool never refuses work.

Live claims decide the next slot: a released claim immediately reopens its
slot, and there is no stored position.

Equal weights give a plain pass in list order. List order is preference, so
put the slots you want preferred first at the top of the list.

Spreading at least two providers across the slots is worth doing deliberately: a
provider-wide rate limit takes out every slot on that provider at once.

## Writing your own

Write `~/.config/lacode/pool.txt` (the flat form above) — that is the whole job.
Or put the same slots in a JSON `~/.config/lacode/pool.json`, or pass `models`
inline from `opencode.jsonc` when you want the list version-controlled beside
the rest of your config:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    ["@lawaty/lacode", {
      "models": {
        "slots": [
          { "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5", "weight": 2 },
          { "model": "opencode/big-pickle", "weight": 1 }
        ]
      }
    }]
  ]
}
```

Whichever provider a slot names must be configured in your own opencode config,
or the model cannot resolve. The pool appends the model id to that provider's
`whitelist` if it has one — the whitelist is an allowlist, so opencode deletes
the model from the provider without it and the agent silently resolves to
nothing — but it cannot invent a provider, and it never writes a whitelist you
did not already have: an absent one already allows every model the provider
offers.

Check what it did with the `pool_status` tool: it prints the resolved source,
each slot with its weight and live load, and which slot the next spawn takes.

### Added

### Changed

  spawn and refilled the moment a claim completed, while the others sat idle.

  the claim, and then failed to abort the session — because the claim was
  released *before* the abort, so a failed kill orphaned the session with
  nothing left to retry it. Kills are verified against the response, retried

  its claim is bound at reap time instead of being lost.

# Cost benchmarks

**This file contains no results.** It explains how to produce your own. The table
below is empty on purpose, and the harness refuses to invent a number to fill it
in.

There is no published savings figure for LaCode, because none has been
independently measured. A number in a README is a claim about somebody's
workload, and yours is not that workload. The plugin changes two things: *which
model does the bulk exploration work*, and *how much of that work has to be done
at all* — agents start from the maintained context map in [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md)
instead of re-deriving the structure of your repository on every task. What that
is worth in money depends entirely on your token mix and on what you compare the
pooled run against. So the harness exists to let you compute the number for
yourself rather than to hand you one to believe.

## What the harness measures

`tests/benchmark/run.mjs` runs one scenario twice — once on your main model, once
on a pooled model — and prints tokens and cost for both.

The comparison only means something because both runs do *identical* work. The
scenario is stated once in the harness and passed to both configurations: the
same four prompts, the same number of calls, a different model doing them.

```
Map the modules that handle authentication and the entry points that reach them.
Find every place a request is authorized and list the file:line for each check.
List the config files that affect routing and the defaults each one sets.
Find the test files covering the auth path and name what each asserts.
```

It is a small, deliberately mechanical scenario. It is not a representative
workload for you, and the harness does not claim it is. Its only job is to make
the two sides of the ratio comparable.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run benchmark` | Simulation (the offline default). No credentials, no network. |
| `npm run benchmark -- --real` | Runs both configurations for real against the `opencode` binary and reads token counts back out of the runs. |
| `npm run benchmark -- --refresh` | Rebuilds `tests/models-snapshot.json` from models.dev first (network), then proceeds as usual. |
| `npm run benchmark -- --out docs/BENCHMARKS.generated.md` | Writes the generated table to the *generated* filename. See below. |

Useful flags for both modes:

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--baseline-model` / `--model` | `anthropic/claude-opus-4-1` | Which model plays "what it would have cost without LaCode". A **name**, never a price. |
| `--calls` | `40` | Simulation only. Number of delegated calls in the task profile. |
| `--input-tokens` | `12000` | Simulation only. Input tokens per call. |
| `--output-tokens` | `1500` | Simulation only. Output tokens per call. |
| `--allow-unknown` | off | Accepts `unknown` in the cost column for a model you named explicitly. Without it the run exits non-zero. |

`--real` additionally honours `OPENCODE_BIN` to locate the opencode binary, and
reads credentials from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_API_KEY` /
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` / `OPENCODE_API_KEY` or from the opencode `auth.json`.

## Simulation vs real

They are different kinds of claim, and the output says which one you are looking
at in every table header.

**Simulation** (the default) is arithmetic over stated assumptions. It takes the
task profile above, multiplies it out, and prices it from the pinned snapshot.
Nothing is executed and nothing is observed. It is a projection, and it is
useful for exactly one thing: seeing how the two rows compare when you change
the profile or the models.

**Real** runs the scenario twice and reads the token counts back out of each
run's own output. That is a measurement of the harness scenario on your machine
on that day. It is still not a measurement of your work.

`--real` degrades rather than failing when it cannot run: with no credentials or
no binary it prints `SKIPPED`, exits 0, and reports nothing. A real run that
fails mid-way exits 3 and refuses to fall through to a projection. If the runs
report no token usage at all, that is an error, not a cost of zero.

## Pricing

Prices come from `tests/models-snapshot.json`, checked in so a run is
reproducible and offline. Regenerate it with `npm run benchmark -- --refresh`
(or `node tests/refresh-models-snapshot.mjs`) when you want current figures.

A model the snapshot has never seen is **skipped with a named reason**. It is
never priced at 0 and never priced at a guess. If you name such a model
explicitly with `--model` / `--baseline-model`, the run exits non-zero and tells
you to refresh or to pass `--allow-unknown`.

This is why the results table below is empty. The pinned snapshot covers the
bundled free preset only; the default baseline model is not in it, so the
default offline run cannot produce an honest ratio.

Nothing in this repository asserts a savings percentage. There is no constant

## Why the generated table is a separate file

`--out` writes to `docs/BENCHMARKS.generated.md`. It **refuses**
`--out docs/BENCHMARKS.md` and exits 2.

That refusal is the point. This file ships inside the npm tarball (`files`
includes `docs`) and is the hand-written explainer. A generated table is a
measurement of one machine on one day, not a claim about the package, so the
explainer is protected and the generated output — which carries a footer
pointing back here — goes to its own gitignored filename.

```bash
npm run benchmark -- --out docs/BENCHMARKS.generated.md
```

# Configuration reference

The plugin options, where the model pool gets its slots, and exactly what LaCode writes into your config. The short version is in the [README](../README.md#configure).

## Pool preset resolution

The slot list is the first of these that yields usable slots:

1. plugin options — `models` in the [tuple](../README.md#configure)
2. `~/.config/lacode/pool.txt` — flat `model [weight] [b:<bucket>] [c:<context>] [notify:on|off]` per line, preferred
3. `~/.config/lacode/pool.json` (its parent directory is created for you)
4. the bundled `presets/free-tier.json`
5. a built-in fallback, so routing always works

A missing, unreadable or structurally broken source falls through to the next and
logs one warning; nothing here throws into opencode. Sources 2–4 are watched: a
change reloads the slot table, re-binds the variant agents and validates every
slot (one real request per model) without a restart. Only a change to the
plugin's own code needs one.

**Any model list is accepted, including paid ones** (US-7). There is no free-tier
allowlist anywhere in the package, and no cost check of any kind: only the
structure is validated. The bundled preset is built from free models because
that is a sensible default, not because the pool requires it.

A slot's `weight` (default 1) is both its concurrency budget and its cap. The
pool fills slots in declaration order in one pass; there is no slot cap, and a
model may appear on more than one line — each line is its own slot with its own
weight. A `tier` key is the deprecated spelling of `weight`.

A slot may also declare a shared quota bucket with `b:<name>` on the line (or a
`bucket` field in JSON). A limit on any member benches the whole bucket, because
the sibling would spend the same exhausted window; without one, the model is its
own bucket. `pool_status` shows each shared bucket's effective capacity.

`c:<context>` is the model's context window in tokens; the router uses it to prefer the smallest model that fits the task, and it is optional for hand-written lines.

Each slot gets a `notify` flag that controls the desktop "rate-limit reset"
notice raised when a slot that was cooling for a quota/rate-limit reason becomes
usable again. The default is **provider-based**: on for `opencode` and
`opencode-go` slots, off for every other provider. On a `pool.txt` line, set
`notify:on` to opt a quiet provider's slot into the notice, or `notify:off` to
silence an `opencode`/`opencode-go` slot; `notify:on`/`notify:off` are accepted
explicitly. In `pool.json`, set `"notify": true` or `"notify": false`
(booleans; `on/off/1/0/yes/no` strings are also accepted). If the same model
appears on several lines, it is announced if **any** of its slots has `notify`
on — to fully silence a model, set `notify:off` on all of its lines. An
invalid `notify` value falls back to the provider default and produces a
warning. The flag gates only the desktop reset notice, not pool routing or
status, and pool files are hot-reloaded so changes take effect without a
restart.

## Modes

Two runtime modes live on the lacode plugin entry and can be toggled from the TUI:

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `/yolo` | Toggle YOLO. Every permission request that would `ask` is approved automatically; an explicit `deny` still wins. |
| `/ykb` | Toggle YKB (You Know Better). The agent is told not to ask questions and to continue with its recommendation. A question that still appears is answered with its `(Recommended)` option, or its first option when none is marked. |
| `/modes` | Show both switches. |

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    ["@lawaty/lacode", { "yolo": true, "ykb": false }]
  ]
}
```

The toggles edit the `yolo` / `ykb` options on the lacode plugin entry in your global opencode config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/opencode.jsonc`), preserving comments. The server reads that file on the next decision — no restart. Turning a mode on also answers requests that are already pending. The lacode plugin entry must already exist in the global config; a project-only entry cannot be toggled. A free-text question with no options is left for the user, since there is no option to choose.


## Which models run which agent

Only the **pool** writes a model onto a pooled agent, from whichever source wins
above. The pooled bases (`explore`, `implement`, `context`)
and their hidden `<base>-<slot>` variants therefore carry no model of their own: a
model written next to an agent would be a second source of truth that silently
wins whenever routing falls through. Spawn a base and let the pool route it.


## ⚠️ Per-agent tool grants must be in your own config

**LaCode cannot grant tools to its agents, and this is not an oversight you can
work around by configuring it.** If you keep a global `"tools"` block in your
config — for example `"tools": { "playwright_*": false }` — then the pooled
exploration and implementation bases (`explore` and `implement`, plus their
hidden `<base>-<slot>` pool variants, one per resolved slot) lose browser access, and **nothing tells them why**: the tool call is simply
refused mid-task. `context` gets no grant either, which is correct — it
writes the context map and has no business in a browser.

opencode folds an agent's `tools` into its permission list **at config-load
time**, while decoding the config — before any plugin runs. A plugin's `config`
hook mutates the already-decoded config, so the fold never re-runs and anything
it puts in `agent.tools` is inert. On opencode 1.18.34/1.18.35, a grant
written in your own config shows two `playwright_*` entries — `deny` then
`allow`, last one winning — while the same grant injected by the plugin shows
only the `deny`. LaCode's other injected
fields are not affected; `permission`, `prompt`, `model`, `description`,
`temperature`, `mode` and `hidden` are all read after the plugin hook runs.

**So if you use a global `"tools"` block, declare the grants yourself:**

```jsonc
{
  "tools": { "playwright_*": false },
  "agent": {
    "explore": { "tools": { "playwright_*": true } },
    "implement": { "tools": { "playwright_*": true } }
  }
}
```

The hidden pool variants (`explore-1`, `implement-2`, …) inherit
nothing here — add a line per variant, or drop the global
deny and scope it to the agents that should not have browser access instead.
Note that you cannot *spawn* a variant by name: the pool rewrites
`explore-1` and friends to their base and routes them, so per-variant
permissions only ever apply to a spawn the plugin routed itself.

The pool files are the exception to the restart rule: editing `pool.txt`,
`pool.json` or the bundled preset is picked up live — the table reloads, the
variant agents re-bind and every slot is validated. A change to `opencode.jsonc`
itself, or to the plugin's code, still needs a restart.

**The delegation path matters.** The pool routes `task` tool calls whose
`subagent_type` is `explore`, `implement` or `context`. A spawn with no
`subagent_type`, an `@explore`/`@implement` mention, or a direct session prompt
naming a base agent does not pass through that hook: it runs opencode's
default/subagent path and inherits the caller's model. Spawn the bare base
through the task tool (`subagent_type: "explore"`), not by mention or variant
name. The plugin logs a warning for the no-`subagent_type` case; the
mention/direct-session case cannot be detected before it runs.


## What gets injected

**One key per base, plus a variant per slot**: the 5 bases `build`, `plan`,
`explore`, `implement`, `context`, one hidden `<base>-<slot>` pool variant per
resolved slot for each of the 3 pooled bases, and the hidden `instructions`
agent — the one writer of the project's root `AGENTS.md`, reachable only from
the `/agent-instructions` command.

`build` and `plan` exist in opencode as built-ins, so on a stock config those
two keys are already taken and merge-without-clobber keeps the built-in — the
LaCode definitions of `build` and `plan` are what you get if you remove the
built-ins of those names first.

**Five keys are deliberately not injected.** `basic` is a byte-for-byte
duplicate of `plan` apart from a pinned model, and `plan` is injected instead.
`expert` pins a specific model and carries a personal benchmark note in its
description — a package cannot ship someone else's provider, quota or benchmark
results — though its escalation ladder still resolves, because the two deep
tiers it escalates to *are* injected. And `explore`, `general` and `implement`
are only `{ "disable": true }` stubs: turning off opencode's built-in agents
is a decision about one person's configuration, not a default a package should
impose on a stranger.

One **field** is deliberately not injected: `tools`, for the load-time-folding
reason explained above. Nothing else the plugin writes into an agent is subject
to it.

**Installation merges, it does not clobber** (US-16). An agent, command or
instruction is added only when that key is absent from your config. A
user-defined agent of the same name is left byte-identical — not patched, not
partially merged. Skips are counted and logged once.

**`enabled: false` turns all of it off** (US-17). No pool model rewriting, no
agent injection, no command injection, no reaper timer armed, no
`~/.config/lacode` directory created.

These three are specified in [docs/USER-STORIES.md](USER-STORIES.md) as
US-7, US-16 and US-17, and each has tests.

# The context map

Every task an agent starts, it starts by exploring: list the directories, open
the entry points, work out which layer a change belongs to, discover which files
call which. On a large repository that is the single most expensive part of the
job, and it happens *every time* — for a question that touches one file, for a
refactor that moves one module, for a session you start after an hour of
something else.

LaCode keeps a short, maintained map of your repository at `.opencode/context/`
and makes every agent read it before exploring. The map answers one question —
**"what should I look at first?"** — and nothing else.

This document is the user-facing description of the system: what the files are,
who writes them, when they are refreshed, and what you can do by hand.

## Why it exists

Agents are stateless between tasks. Anything an agent learns about your
codebase in one session is discarded at the end of it, and re-derived — at full
price — by the next agent. Writing the findings down once, in a form small
enough to read in one call, is what turns that repeated cost into a single
upfront one.

The mechanism is deliberately narrow, because a map that costs more to read than
the exploration it replaces is worse than no map:

- **Conclusions, not inventories.** "`OrderService` is the application boundary
  for order mutations", not "there is a file called OrderService in
  `src/orders/`". The cartographer is forbidden by name from writing directory
  listings, copying source, or restating what the README already says.
- **One file per question.** Five navigation files, each with a defined scope, so
  an agent reads one of them rather than all of them.
- **Canonical entry points.** The highest-value thing in the map is a short
  "Start here" list per subsystem: the canonical files an agent should open, each
  with a one-phrase reason.
- **It links out.** Your project's own README, ADRs and docs are authoritative
  and are not duplicated here.

On cost: the saving is in **tokens not spent re-discovering structure**, and it
is paid by exploration tokens rather than by the expensive main model — the
cartographer that maintains the map runs on a pooled model like every other
subagent. **No savings percentage is published here, because none has been
independently measured.** A number derived from somebody else's repository and
token mix is not a claim about yours; see [BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md) for the
harness that produces a number for your own workload.

## The files in the map

`.opencode/context/` holds the five navigation files below:

| File | What belongs in it |
| --- | --- |
| `architecture.md` | The high-level shape: layers, boundaries, entry points, dependency rules. Read this for an architectural question. |
| `contexts.md` | The major subsystems. For each: what it is for, where to start reading it, what it depends on, what must not change while you are in there. Read this for a subsystem question. |
| `conventions.md` | Repository-specific rules: naming, module layout, error handling, testing, persistence. Read this before writing code, not after. |
| `workflows.md` | The few runtime flows worth tracing end to end — how a request becomes a mutation, how a plugin hook reaches the thing it hooks. Read this when you need to know what actually happens at runtime. |
| `decisions.md` | Architectural constraints that bind future work and that the repository's own decision log does not already record. Each entry states the constraint and points at the page or path that owns it. Capped at 120 non-blank lines; decision records and deliberation are not copied here. |

The project's root `AGENTS.md` is the standing-instructions home: the client's
own statement of intent, what they want worked on and how they want it
approached. It sits outside the map, is per-clone and not committed, and has
no prescribed structure. It has exactly one writer — the hidden `instructions`
agent, reachable only from the `/agent-instructions` command.

Files the user or the plan explicitly names always win over the map. The map is
a shortcut to the right starting point, not an authority. When it disagrees with
**code**, the code is right and the map is wrong. When it disagrees with a
**project page**, neither side is automatically right: the map may be current
and the page stale (that has happened). The disagreement is reported and marked
`[disputed]`; the page's owner resolves it. The cartographer never silently
overwrites either side.

## The entry contract

Every navigation entry has one shape, in every file:

```markdown
- [binding] The operative rule, in at most three non-blank lines. — See `docs/DESIGN.md` §The two halves (verified 2026-10-26)
```

- **A provenance marker.** `[binding]` is a constraint established against the
  source and exempt from age expiry. `[provisional]` is an inference or an
  unverified claim and expires 30 days after `verified`. `[disputed]` records a
  map/page disagreement and is kept, reported, and exempt from age until the
  owner resolves it. There is no second confidence dialect.
- **The rule, not the deliberation.** No Context / Decision / Consequences /
  Alternatives blocks, status lines, or decision records. A reader needs the
  constraint, not the meeting that produced it.
- **A pointer.** A fact whose home is a page cites the page **and** its section
  (`docs/DESIGN.md §Retention`). A fact whose home is code cites the path, with
  an optional line or symbol. No pointer means the content has no source in the
  tree — it is reported as unarchived, never emitted as though it were derived.
- **A verification date.** `(verified YYYY-MM-DD)` drives both the lifecycle and
  the drift check.

Every file has a hard cap, counted in **non-blank lines**: architecture 150,
contexts 200, conventions 150, workflows 150, decisions 120. Lines are the unit
because they are what a reader pays for, they bound an entry that wraps to three
lines, and the validator can count them exactly; an entry count does not bound
cost, and a token count needs a tokenizer and is model-specific. The cap is
enforced by a post-generation validator, not only by the prompt.

A `[provisional]` entry in any navigation file is dropped 30 days after its
`verified` date unless it is re-verified. `[binding]` and `[disputed]` never
expire by age. An entry whose cited source no longer exists is **never**
auto-dropped: it may be the only copy, so it is reported as unarchived and kept.
Only provisional entries whose source still resolves are eligible for the sweep.
The arithmetic lives in `src/lib/map-schema.ts`; the cartographer writes the
shape, code decides what has aged out.

The map is **local and untracked**. It describes *your* checkout on *this*
machine, so committing it would churn on every session that edits a file, and
syncing it to another host would push a description of one machine's projects
onto hosts that have different ones. If you see `.opencode/context/` in a diff,
something has gone wrong.

## How it stays current

The `context` agent maintains the map. It runs in two ways: on its own,
after a session that changed something, and on demand through the three
commands — both of which go through the same agent, so they behave the same way.

### Automatically

After a **root** session goes idle, and only if that session edited a file
inside the project, LaCode starts a `context` run:

1. It collects the paths the session touched, dropping anything generated,
   vendored or outside the project (`node_modules`, `dist`, `coverage`,
   `.git`, and — importantly — the map itself, so the cartographer's own writes
   never trigger another run).
2. It picks `bootstrap` or `update` from what is on disk: if
   `.opencode/context/` does not exist, the run builds the map from scratch;
   if it exists, the run updates it.
3. It borrows a slot from the same pool every other subagent uses, creates a
   session, and hands it the changed paths as *starting context* — not as an
   exhaustive list and not as an instruction to document all of them.

Three things deliberately do **not** trigger a run: a session that edited
nothing, a subagent going idle (they go idle constantly, mid-task), and a second
run within ten minutes of the last one.

An update defaults to *no edit*. A changed file is not a changed fact:
formatting, local renames, added tests and dependency bumps rarely alter what
the map should say. The cartographer is told to edit only when the work
introduced or revealed something that will help a future agent — a new boundary,
a new or moved entry point, a changed workflow, a new convention, an
architectural decision, an undocumented invariant — and to report
"no update needed" otherwise.

After the turn ends, the plugin applies the per-file lifecycle and then audits
the map. The audit is **report-only**: it never rewrites a claim and never
deletes an entry whose source is gone. It checks the schema, each file's line
budget, dangling paths and `§sections`, a numeric claim absent from its cited
source, a possible negation conflict, a source modified after its `verified`
date, tables and fenced blocks (restatements), duplicate rules across files,
archive-of-record language, and whether each file still answers its charter. A
failure is a loud `error` in the log; it is what turns the prompt's rules into a
gate. The deterministic half is `src/lib/map-schema.ts`; the semantic drift pass
is the cartographer's, and it reports a page disagreement instead of picking a
side.

If the map is missing entirely, nothing breaks: agents run the check, find no
`.opencode/context/`, and explore from scratch. What tells them to run the check
is an entry appended to your config's `instructions` array: your own entries are
kept as they are, and a marked entry goes after them unless one of your entries
already carries its marker or its opt-out. LaCode appends two such entries, each
governed by its own pair — the context-map rule
(`<!-- lacode:context-map-instruction:v1 -->`, opt out with
`<!-- lacode:context-map-instruction:off -->`) and the rule that documentation
states the current state (`<!-- lacode:current-state-rule:v1 -->`, opt out with
`<!-- lacode:current-state-rule:off -->`). One opt-out suppresses only the rule
it names.

### On demand

```bash
/context-init      # build the map, or verify and refresh an existing one
/context-update    # incremental refresh; accepts a focus, e.g. /context-update src/payments
/context-review    # audit it for staleness, contradictions, duplication and bloat
```

All three delegate to the same agent, which is why they are consistent with the
automatic run rather than a separate mechanism. `/context-review` treats
everything outside `.opencode/context/` as read-only: it fixes the map, never
your source.

If you have defined a command of the same name, yours wins and is left exactly
as you wrote it — the same merge-without-clobber rule the agents follow.

The same code owns the navigation files' lifecycle, but it may only **drop** an
entry that is `[provisional]`, past its 30-day window, and whose cited source
still exists. It never drops a binding constraint or disputed entry, and it
never drops an entry with no source — that is the one case where the map may be
the only copy. The plugin is not a second writer of the map in the permission
sense: `context` is still the only **agent** that writes it. The lifecycle is
housekeeping by code, applied after a run and then audited.

## One writer

Only `context` writes the map. Every other agent is told never to edit
it, and to say in its final report if its work revealed something that belongs
in there. The cartographer, in turn, is denied permission to write anything
outside the map — not by convention, but by an `edit` rule that allows
`.opencode/context/**` and nothing else.

The rule runs in both directions. The agents that *could* write anywhere else in
the repository — the root `build` agent and both implement tiers — carry the
mirror image of the cartographer's grant: `"*": "allow"` followed by a `deny` on
`.opencode/context/**`, so they edit everything except the map. Enforcement is
two mechanisms at once, and both are load-bearing: the injected instruction
naming the one writer, and the permission rule — a permission denial tells an
agent nothing about what it should have done instead.

This exists because two writers produce a map that is neither current nor
trustworthy. Concurrent sessions rewriting the same files produce
contradictions that no later reader can resolve, and the reader has no way to
tell which version is newer.

Ordering in those rules is not cosmetic. opencode resolves a file permission by
taking the **last** matching rule in declaration order, with no specificity
sorting: a `deny` written above a broad `"*": "allow"` loses. LaCode therefore
writes every narrow rule last, in both files (`src/agents.ts` and your own
`opencode.jsonc`), and `src/lib/writer-rule.ts` checks that order rather than
grepping for the word `allow` — which is what stops a correctly-placed deny from
being reported as a hole.

The rule has a sharp edge worth knowing about: **opencode evaluates a file
permission against the path relative to the project root, not the absolute path
the tool was given.** A rule written as `*/.opencode/context/**` matches an
absolute path and therefore matches nothing at all. Both spellings are therefore
required — `.opencode/context/**` for a normally-rooted project and
`*/.opencode/context/**` for one rooted at `/` — and LaCode ships both. At
startup the plugin checks your config for that, and logs an error naming the
rules it saw if neither form would ever fire.

### The residual risk: a subdirectory worktree

Those patterns are matched against `relative(worktree, filepath)`, and the
spelling that is supposed to fire depends on where the worktree root sits:

- **worktree = repo root** → the map is `.opencode/context/architecture.md`, and
  `.opencode/context/**` fires. `*/.opencode/context/**` does not.
- **worktree = `/`** → the map is `home/<you>/…/.opencode/context/…`, and only
  `*/.opencode/context/**` fires.

Shipping both spellings covers those two. What it does **not** cover is a third
case: if the worktree is a subdirectory rather than the repo root — you opened
opencode one directory down from the repository root — then the evaluated path
gains a prefix that matches *neither* pattern. Both rules match nothing, the
deny against other agents silently stops applying, and **nothing is reported**,
because a rule matching nothing is not an error in opencode's evaluator and the
startup check has no way to see a worktree it was not told about.

How to detect it: open opencode from the repository root, not from a
subdirectory of it. If `ls .opencode/context` from your shell's current
directory does not list the map files, your shell is not at the root and
neither is opencode's worktree. The cost of getting it wrong is not a crash —
it is a map maintained only by prompt, with no mechanism enforcing who writes it.

The symptom is silence: the cartographer's writes are denied without an error,
its run reports success, and the map quietly stops changing. So a run that
changed nothing on disk is reported as a warning, not as a success: if you see
`auto update finished without changing the map` repeatedly, the first thing
to check is that permission rule, not the map's content.

## What you will see in the log

| Line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `borrowed pool slot N (model, wW) for auto update` | A refresh started, on a pooled model. |
| `auto update finished` | The run completed and changed at least one map file. |
| `auto update finished without changing the map` | Nothing landed. Either nothing needed saying, or the cartographer could not write. |
| `auto update failed: …` | The run errored. The paths it was given are queued again for the next window, so the work is not lost. |
| `map lifecycle: dropped N expired provisional entr… from <file>` | The code sweep dropped an entry past its 30-day window. Binding and disputed entries are never dropped. |
| `context map validation passed` | Every file is in schema and within budget, every pointer resolves, and the drift checks found nothing. |
| `context map validation failed: N issue(s)` | The run's map is off schema or over budget, cites a missing path/section, restates a page, or has a possible contradiction. The map is **not** rewritten; the log names up to 20 issues and the paths to fix. |
| `context map is not writable: …` | Your config's one-writer rule does not match the path opencode evaluates. Nothing will update until you fix it. |
| `context map has more than one writer: …` | An agent other than `context` would be granted the map. The offending agent and the winning rule are named. |
