# Install and troubleshooting

Everything about getting LaCode loaded, and what to do when it silently is not. The one-line install is in the [README](../README.md#getting-started); this page is for the rest of it.

A plugin that fails to load is silent — opencode starts normally, prints nothing, logs nothing, and the agents are simply not there. Start at [If the agents are missing](#if-the-agents-are-missing).

## Where it is installed

opencode installs npm plugins itself, into one directory per specifier under its
cache — not into your project's `node_modules`, and not from anywhere a global
npm install put them. Ask opencode where that cache is instead of assuming,
because where it lives differs by platform:

```bash
opencode debug paths
```

It prints the directories opencode is using on this machine — config, data, log
and the rest. Find the **cache** line and append
`/packages/<specifier>/node_modules/` to the path it reports. On Linux with no
`XDG_CACHE_HOME` set, that comes out as, for example:

```
~/.cache/opencode/packages/@lawaty/lacode@latest/node_modules/
```

**That last line is an illustration of one platform's layout, not a path to
copy.** Where the same cache root sits on another operating system is not
something this document should guess at — read it from `opencode debug paths`
and use what it prints.

To inspect what a specifier actually resolved to, list its directory under that
cache root. An **empty** directory with no `node_modules` inside it means the
install failed — almost always an unpublished or misspelled package — and
opencode starts normally **without** the plugin. A **populated** directory there
means the install succeeded and tells you nothing at all about whether the
plugin was loaded; that is the next section, and telling those two apart is the
whole reason for reading it.


## If the agents are missing

A plugin that fails to load is silent: opencode starts normally, prints nothing,
logs nothing, and the agents are simply not there. Work down this. Every step
below is written to hold whichever opencode version you are running — none of
them depends on knowing the answer in advance.

**1 — Write the bare specifier and restart.**

```json
{ "plugin": ["@lawaty/lacode"] }
```

Nothing here hot-reloads, so the restart is part of the step, not a footnote.

**2 — Check whether the plugin loaded.**

```bash
opencode agent list | grep -E '^(explore|implement|context)'
```

A working install prints `explore`, `implement` and `context`, each with the
hidden `-1`..`-4` pool variants alongside. If the
grep returns nothing and the list holds only opencode's own built-ins, the plugin
did not load. Run it in the same shell environment opencode runs in — an
`agent list` under a different `HOME` or `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` tests a different
machine. **If the agents are listed, stop here: the one line above is the whole
install**, and nothing further in this section applies to you.

**3 — Decide which failure you are looking at.** Inspect the package directory
under the cache root from
[Where it is installed](#where-it-is-installed), and also check that `plugin`
really is in the config file opencode reads.

- **Empty** (no `node_modules` inside): the install failed — check the package
  name, and that it is published. There is nothing to load yet.
- **Populated**: the install worked and the loader dropped the plugin. Go to
  step 4. These two look identical from the outside, which is why this step
  exists.

**4 — If the install worked and the agents are still missing, point the loader
at the built file.** Add a second entry; leave the bare name in place:

```json
{
  "plugin": [
    "@lawaty/lacode",
    "file:///ABSOLUTE-PATH-FROM-debug-paths/packages/@lawaty/lacode@latest/node_modules/@lawaty/lacode/dist/index.js"
  ]
}
```

`ABSOLUTE-PATH-FROM-debug-paths` is a placeholder to be replaced, not a
directory: take the cache path `opencode debug paths` reports for **your**
machine and put it in front of `/packages/…`. It must be an absolute path with
`$HOME` already expanded and no `~` left in it. Re-derive it after a cache wipe
or a reinstall — the directory is keyed by specifier, so it moves when the
version does.

Why keep both entries instead of swapping the bare name out:

- The bare name is what makes opencode install the package into its cache, and
  therefore what creates the path the `file://` entry points at.
- The `file://` entry is what actually loads the plugin.
- They **cannot double-inject** on opencode 1.18.35, where the bare name
  contributes nothing at all: the pair loads the plugin exactly once. On any
  other version this is untested, which is precisely why step 4 is something you
  take *because* step 2 showed the agents missing, and never on the expectation
  that it would help.

**5 — Restart, and expect two restarts after a cache wipe.** The first start
installs the package and creates the path the `file://` entry points at, but a
path that does not exist at startup is a path that cannot be loaded in that same
run. The second start finds it and loads the plugin. After that it is steady
state.

This package also publishes `main` and an `exports["./server"]` entry pointing at
the same built file, because those are two of the shapes a plugin loader
resolving an entry point consults. They are forward-compatibility metadata and
they cost nothing — but they do **not** fix this on 1.18.35: adding either one to
the *installed* cache copy leaves the bare specifier loading nothing. Whether
they help on any other version is unknown. Use the `file://` entry.


## Which opencode versions this is known on

Exactly one version is measured, and the procedure above is deliberately
not built around that fact. Treat this table as the evidence it is, which is one
row wide.

| opencode version | bare spec loads? | `file://` needed? | evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.18.35 | No — installs the package, then silently drops it | Yes | Measured on 1.18.35: a populated cache directory, zero agents injected, no error and no log line; the `file://` entry loads the full agent set. |
| Any other version | **Unknown** | **Unknown** | No other opencode version is covered by this table, in either direction. |

**If your version is not the one measured here, follow the procedure above
rather than reading this table as coverage of your build**: each step stands on
its own, and step 2 tells you which situation you are in before any
version-specific advice is relevant.


## macOS

The plugin runs on macOS. It is plain JavaScript with no native dependency, and
what the package publishes is the built JavaScript rather than TypeScript
sources, so nothing about loading it is Linux-only. Use the procedure above
unchanged.

Three things differ, and all three are worth reading rather than assuming:

- **Paths.** Do not copy a cache path out of this document — the example under
  [Where it is installed](#where-it-is-installed) is one platform's layout. Run
  `opencode debug paths` and build the `file://` entry from what it reports.
  This page deliberately does not name a macOS cache root: where opencode keeps
  it on a Mac has not been established here, and a plausible-looking guess is
  worse than an instruction to look.
- **Notifications** are delivered through `osascript`, or through
  `terminal-notifier` when `osascript` is not installed, rather than through the
  Linux `notify-send` (US-26). `lacode doctor` reports which channel your machine
  would actually use.
- **The repository's shell scripts are Linux-only by design**, and are not in the
  published package. They drive one person's SSH topology, so each is on the side
  it belongs to:

- **Remote hosts are plain npm clients.** A remote host installs the plugin the
  same way (`opencode plugin @lawaty/lacode -g`); there is nothing to rsync. The
  notification hop is a direct ssh (`ControlMaster` + `ControlPersist`) set up
  once with `lacode tunnel setup` — no reverse forward, no listening port, no
  systemd unit. See [Remote hosts](../README.md#remote-hosts) and docs/TUNNEL.md.
- The repo carries the author's personal, Linux-only reverse-forward tooling
  (`bin/oc`, `bin/oc-notify`, `bin/oc-notify-receiver`,
  `bin/oc-sync`). None of it is in the published package, and none of it is needed
  for the npm-client path above.

**The test suite runs on macOS.** It is written to pass on a Mac as well as on
Linux, so "it works on a Mac" is a supported claim rather than an intention. The
few checks that exercise the Linux-only shell scripts above skip themselves on a
machine that cannot run them, naming the reason — a bash 3.2 with no `mapfile`,
or no GNU `timeout` — rather than passing silently or failing confusingly.


## The `lacode` CLI

The package also ships the `lacode` CLI (`notify`, `forward`, `doctor`, `feedback`,
`version`, `update`, `receive`, `tunnel setup`) — see
[Remote hosts](../README.md#remote-hosts). The plugin install does **not** put it on your
`PATH`; run it from the package's `node_modules/.bin`, or install just the CLI
globally with `npm i -g @lawaty/lacode` if you want the bare command. (That
global install is for the command only — it is still never what makes the plugin
load.)


## What the install gives you

Two things are worth knowing about what npm actually hands you:

- **`@opencode-ai/plugin` is a peer dependency.** It is not vendored into this
  package and never will be: a second copy of the SDK inside the tarball would
  mean opencode and the plugin holding two different module instances, and
  instance identity is what plugin state hangs on. npm installs the peer for you;
  if you install with a tool that does not, install `@opencode-ai/plugin` at the
  same version yourself.
- **You get compiled JavaScript, not TypeScript sources.** The tarball ships
  `dist/`, built from `src/` at pack time (`prepack` runs the build, so a stale
  `dist/` cannot be published). This is not a preference: node strips types
  natively from 22.18 but **refuses to for files under `node_modules`**, so a
  package that ships `.ts` fails on install — `lacode --help` exits with
  `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING`. A published package cannot
  depend on its consumer's loader being lenient.

# OmniRoute gateway integration

[OmniRoute](https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute) is a local OpenAI-compatible gateway that routes a request across many providers with fallback and "combos". LaCode can register it as an opencode provider. It is **off by default**. The summary is in the [README](../README.md#configure); this page is the full reference, including a combo ordered for latency that is worth applying on a new client.

## Configuring OmniRoute

[OmniRoute](https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute) is a local
OpenAI-compatible AI gateway (default `http://localhost:20128/v1`) that routes a
request across many providers with fallback and "combos". LaCode can register it
as an opencode provider for you. It is **off by default**: if you do not set
`omniroute.enabled: true`, nothing below happens and LaCode makes no request.

**Setting it up on a client machine.** Four steps, in this order:

1. Install OmniRoute, then make it stay up: run `omniroute autostart enable`
   once. That writes a systemd user unit in a headless session, or an XDG
   autostart entry in a graphical one, and OmniRoute supervises itself from
   there on. Its gateway listens on `http://localhost:20128/v1`. The gateway's
   lifecycle is **the client's responsibility**: LaCode never starts, supervises
   or stops it, it only probes it. The gateway must therefore already be
   running **before** you start opencode — one that is down at startup is
   disabled for that run, and the integration is per-run.
2. Add the plugin block to your opencode config:
   `["@lawaty/lacode", { "omniroute": { "enabled": true, "apiKey": "<your omniroute key>", "combo": "auto", "models": [] } }]`
   `auto` is the zero-config default, but on a free tier it often resolves to a
   slow chain. [A tested fast combo](#a-tested-fast-combo-free-mix) below is
   ordered for latency and is worth applying on a new client.
3. Optionally, to route pooled work through it, add an `omniroute/<id>` slot to
   `~/.config/lacode/pool.txt` exactly as you would any other provider. The
   integration gives it no special precedence, priority or weight — its place and
   weight in the pool are whatever you configure. `pool.txt` is optional user
   config; the bundled default preset does **not** include OmniRoute.
4. **Restart opencode.** Nothing here hot-reloads.

With `models: []` and `combo: "auto"`, the plugin registers exactly one model,
`omniroute/auto`, which then appears in the model picker for any agent — no
hand-maintained model list.

The full option set, for reference:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    ["@lawaty/lacode", {
      "omniroute": {
        "enabled": true,
        "baseURL": "http://localhost:20128/v1",
        "apiKey": "sk_omniroute",          // optional; OMNIROUTE_API_KEY overrides it
        "combo": "static-best-free",        // optional: let OmniRoute do the routing
        "models": ["cc/claude-sonnet-4-6", "gemini-3-flash"], // hard allowlist
        "tiers": {
          "primary": ["cc/claude-sonnet-4-6"],
          "backup": ["gemini-3-flash"]
        },
        "stickyPerSession": true,
        "healthCheck": true,
        "timeoutMs": 5000
      }
    }]
  ]
}
```

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `false` | Turns the integration on. |
| `baseURL` | `http://localhost:20128/v1` | Gateway base URL, normalised to exactly one `/v1`. |
| `apiKey` | — | Bearer key. **`OMNIROUTE_API_KEY` overrides this value.** The key is never logged. |
| `combo` | — | An OmniRoute combo id (or `auto`) to expose as a selectable model even though the gateway does not list it. It leads the provider's own model list — an OmniRoute-side detail, unrelated to pool order. |
| `models` | — | A **hard allowlist**: only these ids are ever exposed, even if the gateway lists more. |
| `tiers` | — | `{ "primary": [...], "backup": [...] }` preference order over models the allowlist already permits. |
| `stickyPerSession` | `true` | Keep a session on one model while that model is healthy. |
| `healthCheck` | `true` | Probe `GET /models` at startup; a failed check disables the integration for that run only. |
| `timeoutMs` | `5000` | Budget for LaCode's own probe and model-cache calls to the gateway. It is not written into the provider options, so it does not bound real traffic — opencode's own default applies there. |

An enabled but invalid block (bad `baseURL`, a non-array `models`, …) is rejected
as a whole: LaCode logs one warning naming the problem and continues exactly as
if the integration were off. It never crashes opencode.

**What it registers.** On the first `config` pass LaCode health-checks the
gateway, reads `GET /models`, filters it through your `models` allowlist (or
exposes everything the gateway lists when no allowlist is set), and writes a
`provider.omniroute` entry — `npm: "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible"` with your
`baseURL` / `apiKey` — so `omniroute/<model-id>` becomes selectable. If you
already have a `provider.omniroute` block, LaCode leaves it completely untouched
and warns; it also never adds a `whitelist`. Because opencode loads
`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` itself, no extra dependency is installed.

**Combo vs. allowlist.** Set `combo` and OmniRoute does the fallback for you
(let it route): the combo leads the exposed models, so opencode can hand a failed
request to the gateway's own fallback chain. Without a combo, LaCode exposes the
allowlist ordered by `tiers` (primary first). Candidate order is `filterModels`
(combo first, then the hard allowlist) followed by `orderByTier`, and that is
all — LaCode picks which model is exposed and in what order; it does not measure
latency or error rate at runtime, and it does not skip a model because it
failed.

**Using OmniRoute in the pool.** The integration only *registers* the provider —
it never touches your pool, and it does not place a slot for you. To route pooled
work (exploration, implementation, cartography) through the gateway, add an
`omniroute/<id>` slot to your pool like any other model:

```
# ~/.config/lacode/pool.txt
omniroute/free-mix
opencode/big-pickle
opencode-go/beam-free
```

OmniRoute is a provider like any other: the pool decides its place and weight,
and neither the pool nor this integration gives it any built-in precedence or
priority — where it sits and how many turns it takes are whatever you configure.
Any `omniroute/<id>` works, provided the id is exposed — by `combo`/`models`, or
the whole catalog when neither is set. Because the plugin writes the pool
nothing, the only thing that changes when the gateway is down is that
`omniroute/<id>` fails; every other slot keeps working. See
[docs/USER-STORIES.md](USER-STORIES.md) US-28.


## A tested fast combo: `free-mix`

`combo: "auto"` is the zero-configuration default, but `auto` inherits whatever
the gateway chooses, and on a busy free tier that is frequently the slowest
chain available. The combo below is ordered for latency rather than for
breadth. Apply it during the "Setting it up on a client machine" steps above
and pooled work is usable straight away, instead of starting from a gateway that
queues for half a minute per call.

```jsonc
{
  "name": "free-mix",
  // Order decides. Do NOT use "weighted" here — weights let the gateway
  // re-shuffle a model that is returning 429 into first position again.
  "strategy": "priority",
  "models": [
    { "model": "gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite",                      "providerId": "gemini" },
    { "model": "gemini/gemini-3.8-flash",                           "providerId": "gemini" },
    { "model": "gemini/gemini-3.7-flash",                           "providerId": "gemini" },
    { "model": "gemini/gemini-3-flash-preview",                     "providerId": "gemini" },
    { "model": "openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free",  "providerId": "openrouter" },
    { "model": "openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free",  "providerId": "openrouter" },
    { "model": "openrouter/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free",     "providerId": "openrouter" },
    { "model": "openrouter/cohere/north-mini-code:free",            "providerId": "openrouter" },
    { "model": "openrouter/poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free",             "providerId": "openrouter" },
    { "model": "openrouter/dots-studio/dots-3-note-preview:free",   "providerId": "openrouter" }
  ]
}
```

Why this order — it is the two free-tier failure modes, a hard reject and a
slow queue-budget timeout:

| Model | Behaviour on a busy free tier | Position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gemini/gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | succeeds on the large majority of calls, ~4.5s median | **first** |
| `gemini-3.8-flash` / `3.7-flash` / `3-flash-preview` | succeed intermittently, but **stall ~30s** on a `503` queue-budget timeout when they do not | next |
| `openrouter/*:free` | **mostly `429`**, but fail *fast* (~1.8s) and occasionally succeed | last, as a cheap final fallback |
| `gemini-2.5-flash`, `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` | **`404` on every attempt** — dead ids | **omitted entirely** |

The ordering matters because a combo pays for *every* step it walks past. Put the
reliable model first and the common case is a single hop; the 30s models sit
behind it where they cost nothing, and the 429s sit last where they give up in
under two seconds.

These free-tier endpoints change availability constantly, so treat the ordering
as a **starting point to re-measure, not a permanent truth**. Re-check it with
OmniRoute's own call logs before assuming it still holds:

```bash
# one timed request through the gateway
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_starttransfer}s\n' \
  -X POST http://localhost:20128/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OMNIROUTE_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"free-mix","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK"}],"max_tokens":10}'

# per-model status + duration, straight from OmniRoute's logs
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, glob, collections
d = "/home/<user>/.omniroute/call_logs/<YYYY-MM-DD>"
g = collections.defaultdict(collections.Counter)
for f in glob.glob(d + "/*.json"):
    try: s = json.load(open(f))["summary"]
    except Exception: continue
    g[s.get("comboStepId")][s.get("status")] += 1
for k, v in sorted(g.items(), key=lambda x: str(x[0])):
    print(f"{str(k)[:44]:44} {dict(v)}")
PY
```

Apply it with the bundled CLI (`PUT /api/combos/<id>` updates in place, so the
combo is never briefly missing):

```bash
omniroute api combos get-api-combos-id- --id <combo-id> --json > free-mix.json
# edit name/strategy/models in free-mix.json, then:
omniroute api combos put-api-combos-id- --id <combo-id> --body @free-mix.json
```

**A note on mid-session switching.** opencode 1.18.34 exposes no hook to change
an agent's main model mid-request, so LaCode cannot swap models inside a running
session; use an OmniRoute `combo` (or `auto`) if you want per-request fallback.
LaCode's selection engine decides which models are exposed and in what order, and
its cooldown/backoff rules are unit-tested.

**Getting a key.** Open the OmniRoute dashboard, go to API Manager / API Keys and
copy a key into `OMNIROUTE_API_KEY` (recommended) or `omniroute.apiKey`. On a
local instance with `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false`, the literal placeholder
`sk_omniroute` is accepted.

**Troubleshooting**

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `omniroute health check failed` at startup | Gateway not running, wrong `baseURL`, or a startup race | Start OmniRoute on `http://localhost:20128` and restart opencode; `omniroute autostart enable` makes that durable across restarts. The integration is disabled for that run only, not permanently. |
| `omniroute health check failed` at startup, then a repeating `cooling omniroute/<id> (hang)` and `Model not found` churn on one slot | OmniRoute was started *after* opencode, and `pool.txt` names an `omniroute/<id>` slot | The integration is off for that run, but the pool still routes to the slot: the request hangs, the reaper cools it for 600s, and the cycle repeats. Start OmniRoute, then restart opencode. |
| `ProviderModelNotFoundError: Model not found` on an id the gateway serves | The id is a valid OmniRoute route but is not in the plugin's `models` allowlist, so the plugin never exposed it | Add the id to `models`, or set it as `combo` — `combo` is registered whether or not the gateway advertises it, so a valid gateway route works there too. A valid gateway route is not automatically an exposed model. |
| `no usable models` | The gateway returned an empty list, or every id was filtered out by `models` | `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $OMNIROUTE_API_KEY" http://localhost:20128/v1/models` and check `models`/`combo` against the returned ids. |
| `401` / `Invalid API key` | `REQUIRE_API_KEY=true` and the key is missing or wrong | Create a key in the dashboard, export `OMNIROUTE_API_KEY`, or set `REQUIRE_API_KEY=false` locally and use `sk_omniroute`. |
| `404` on a URL containing `/v1/v1/` | A `baseURL` that already carried `/v1` was given twice | LaCode normalises this, so it should not come from LaCode; check a hand-written `provider.omniroute` block, which LaCode leaves untouched. |
| Provider registered but models are missing | You already had `provider.omniroute` | Remove it and let LaCode write it, or add the models yourself — LaCode never modifies an existing provider. |
| Pooled work still runs on the bundled models | The gateway was unhealthy/disabled at startup, or you have no `omniroute/…` slot in your pool | Check the startup log for `omniroute health check failed` / `no usable models`, then add `omniroute/<model>` to `pool.txt` (or `pool.json`) to route pooled work through the gateway. |

# Notifications from remote hosts

opencode runs on your laptop. It also runs on the remote hosts you ssh into. A
notification raised on a remote host has nowhere to go: that machine has no
desktop, no session bus, and possibly no `notify-send`. This is the hop that
gets it back.

## The shape

```
  remote host                                   your desktop
  ┌──────────────────┐   direct ssh             ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ opencode session │   (ControlPersist)       │  lacode receive        │
  │      │           │ ───────────────────────► │  (authorized_keys      │
  │      ▼           │   ONE argument:          │   forced command)      │
  │ lacode notify    │   title\nmessage\n       │      │                 │
  │                  │   urgency\nicon\nsound   │      ▼                 │
  │                  │   \nrequestID            │  notify-send /         │
  │                  │                          │  osascript             │
  │      ▲           │ ◄─────────────────────── │                        │
  │                  │   the clicked button's   │                        │
  │                  │   name, on the forced    │                        │
  │                  │   command's stdout       │                        │
  └──────────────────┘                          └────────────────────────┘
```

**Direct ssh, one warm connection.** The hop is a plain `ssh` to the desktop with
`ControlMaster=auto` + `ControlPersist`, so the first notification opens the
connection and every later one rides it. There is no reverse forward, no
listening port, no systemd unit and nothing to sync: the plugin owns the
transport, and it exists only while opencode runs — which is the only time a
notification matters.

**One argument, not six.** ssh concatenates everything after the host into a
single command string, and a forced command starts with *no* positional
parameters. A sender that passes six quoted arguments arrives as the single
string `"a b c d e f"`; a receiver reading `$1..$6` sees six empty strings,
falls back to six defaults, and pops up a blank notification. So the payload
crosses as one newline-delimited argument:

```
title\nmessage\nurgency\nicon\nsound\nrequestID
```

Six fields — `title`, `message`, `urgency`, `icon`, `sound`, `requestID`.
`sound` is `none`, `done`, `question`, `permission` or `error`. The request id
is **last**, and it is opaque: it is never shown to you, never passed to a
command, and never used to build an argument — the only thing it decides is
whether the notification carries buttons. A sender that stops at `icon`
simply leaves the rest empty, and an empty or unrecognised name is `none`, so a
four-field payload is a valid one; a payload with fewer than six fields carries
no request id at all, and therefore no buttons, so an older sender still works
against a receiver that expects six.

Newline is safe as the delimiter because both ends strip control characters from
the free-text fields before assembling or reading it, and `urgency`, `icon` and
`sound` come from whitelists. No field can contain the delimiter, so a message
full of spaces, quotes or `*` survives intact.

## The way back

The hop was one-way until now: the notification went up to the desktop and
nothing came back, because there was nothing on the wire to carry an answer.
It is two-way now, and what made it two-way was not a new mechanism. **The
desktop end is an ssh forced command, so its stdout comes back down the same
ssh connection the notification went up.** That channel was already there and
nobody used it: a forced command's stdout is carried to whoever opened the
connection, so the answer rides home on the connection that is already open —
no second connection, no listener, no port, no new key, no HTTP server.

A permission notification that carries a request id is raised with three
buttons: **Allow once**, **Always allow** and **Deny**. `notify-send` waits
for the click and prints the chosen button's *name* on stdout — `once`,
`always` or `reject`, and "reject" is opencode's own word for deny, not ours.
The name needs no translation: it is already one of the values the server
accepts as a permission reply. The plugin reads it off the helper's stdout and
answers the permission through opencode's own reply route.

Two things follow from the shape. An **empty** stdout means the popup was
dismissed without a button being chosen: nothing is answered, and the
permission is left exactly as it was. And a permission that was **already
answered** — most often in the terminal — comes back as "not found" rather
than as a failure, because the user did what they had to do and clicking a
stale notification is not an error.

The wait is bounded: ten minutes on the desktop side, and the hop's own
deadline is stretched to outlast it, because an answer cut off by a timeout is
worse than no answer at all.

The buttons are **Linux-only**. `notify-send --action` is the only one of the
three channels that can offer one — `osascript` and `terminal-notifier` have no
action support — so a macOS desktop gets a plain notice, and the answer there
still has to be given in the terminal.

## Setting it up

Once, on the **remote host** (where opencode runs):

```bash
lacode tunnel setup
```

It generates the dedicated key (`~/.ssh/lacode_notify` by default) and prints the
environment to export there, and the single `authorized_keys` line to add on the
desktop:

```
OC_LOCAL_USER=<desktop user>
OC_LOCAL_HOST=<desktop hostname>
OC_NOTIFY_KEY=~/.ssh/lacode_notify
```

On the **desktop**, add the printed line to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`:

```
restrict,command="lacode receive" ssh-ed25519 AAAA… lacode-notify
```

`restrict` does the security work: no shell, no PTY, no agent forwarding, no port
forwarding. The key can do exactly one thing — hand one notification to
`lacode receive` — and nothing else. Use the absolute path to `lacode` if it is
not on the forced command's `PATH`.

## Sending

The CLI picks the transport by where it is running — `SSH_CLIENT` or `SSH_TTY`
means remote, so it forwards; otherwise it delivers locally through whichever
desktop notifier this platform has: `notify-send` on Linux, `osascript` on macOS,
with `terminal-notifier` as the macOS fallback when `osascript` is missing.

```bash
lacode notify "build finished" "4 files changed" normal dialog-information
lacode notify "question" "which database should I use?" critical dialog-warning done
lacode forward web-01 -- systemctl --user status something
lacode doctor
```

SOUND is optional and last: `none`, `done`, `question`, `permission` or `error`,
one bundled tone per outcome. Leave it off and nothing plays; the line above
without a fifth word is correct.

`LACODE_REQUEST_ID` in the environment is the one thing that makes a send
actionable: it is the permission request id, it is opaque, and it is set on the
helper by the plugin rather than by you. A send with it carries the three
buttons on Linux and prints the name of the clicked one on stdout; a send
without it is an ordinary notice that prints nothing.

A plain `notify` is fire-and-forget by design. An unreachable desktop, a
missing key, no notifier installed at all — all of them print a warning on
stderr and exit 0. A notification must never be able to fail the process that
tried to send one; an agent must not go down because a laptop went to sleep.
`forward` is the exception: it exits with the remote's status, because its
caller wants to know. An **actionable** notify is the other exception, and it
is bounded rather than open-ended: it waits for the click, because the answer
is the whole point of it, and it still exits 0 whatever happens.

On macOS the text is passed to `osascript` as arguments to an `on run argv`
handler, never spliced into the script source — a session title is not trusted
input. `lacode doctor` prints the channel that would actually run, so it is
useful on a Mac rather than reporting only whether a Linux binary is installed.

## The desktop side: `lacode receive`

`lacode receive` is the forced command. It reads the newline payload from
`$SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND`, sanitizes each field again at the trust boundary, and
delivers locally through the platform channel — `notify-send` on Linux,
`osascript`/`terminal-notifier` on macOS. Because it delegates to the same local
channel as a local send, **the desktop half is not Linux-only**: a Mac desktop
receives notifications too.

The buttons are the exception to that. Only `notify-send` can offer one, so a
payload with a request id is an actionable notification on Linux and a plain
notice — one that prints nothing — on macOS. What the receiver prints on stdout
is the chosen button's name, and that stdout is what carries the answer back up
the connection (see [The way back](#the-way-back)). The request id itself is
never passed to a command and never printed — only its emptiness is ever
tested.

It never forwards: `SSH_CLIENT` is set for a forced command as well, so it calls
the local channel directly rather than `notify()` (which would loop back).

It plays the sound too, and that is not decoration. The notification is rendered
on the desktop, so that is the only place a tone can be heard: the remote host
runs the session and has no speakers. The name is validated against the sound
whitelist at the same trust boundary as `urgency` and `icon`, and the receiver
looks the file up in the package's own `sounds/` directory — the sender's word
never becomes a path. `afplay` plays it on macOS, `paplay`, `aplay` or
`pw-play` on Linux, and a machine with none of them gets the notification
regardless.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OC_LOCAL_USER` | *(unset)* | The desktop user the hop authenticates as. **Required for the remote hop.** |
| `OC_LOCAL_HOST` | *(unset)* | Desktop hostname for the direct ssh hop. The default; set it and no reverse forward or port is used. |
| `OC_NOTIFY_KEY` | `~/.ssh/lacode_notify` | The dedicated key. Never a personal key. |
| `OC_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` | `5000` | Ceiling on the hop. |
| `OC_SSH_TIMEOUT_MS` | `30000` | Ceiling on `forward`. |
| `OC_TUNNEL_PORT` | `10022` | Reverse-forward listener port. Used when `OC_LOCAL_HOST` is unset. |

`OC_LOCAL_USER` is read rather than probed on purpose. `id -un` on a remote
account frequently returns `root`, and a dbus path built from that reaches
nobody's desktop. Guessing the desktop user is worse than failing.

`LACODE_SOUND` is deliberately absent from that table, and not by oversight:
every `OC_*` name above is read by the hop — either by `lacode notify` or by the
ssh call it makes — and `lacode tunnel setup` prints what it exports. Sound is
not that. It is a plugin-level mute switch read by the process running opencode
(`sound: false` is the same switch in the config), so listing it here would send
you to export a variable into a hop environment where nothing looks at it. It is
documented with the other plugin options in the README. Set it to `0`, `false`,
`off` or `no` to silence notifications; anything else — a typo included — leaves
sound on, because a misspelt variable must not be how you turn a feature off.

`LACODE_REQUEST_ID` is absent for the same kind of reason, and it is not yours
to set either: the plugin puts the permission request id on the helper
process, and the helper carries it as the payload's sixth field. The hop only
ever asks whether it is there.

## The reverse forward

A host that sets `OC_TUNNEL_PORT` and leaves `OC_LOCAL_HOST` unset reaches the
desktop through a reverse forward: `sendRemote` falls back to an ssh call to
`localhost:<port>`, where a `systemd --user` unit on the desktop holds an
`ssh -R` forward open and delivers to a `notify-send`-only bash receiver
(`bin/oc-notify-receiver`). That receiver is the Linux end of the hop: it
delivers through `notify-send`, and libnotify is a Linux thing, so a Mac cannot
be this end of the tunnel.

The way back works the same way here: the receiver's stdout comes back down
the forward, on the connection the notification went up, so a click on one of
the three buttons is carried home the same way it is on the direct hop.

# LaCode — User Stories

> Ultimate opencode setup for Go users

Every story below is a behavioural contract, not a feature wish. Each one is
traceable to a pain point the author actually hit, and each carries acceptance
criteria written so that a test can assert them mechanically. Every row of the
Coverage table has a test file.

**Reading the criteria.** Every criterion is written as *Given … When … Then …
* so that it maps to one test case. "Given" is a state or fixture, "When" is a
single action (usually a hook invocation or a script run), "Then" is an
observable result — a routing decision, a file on disk, an exit status, a log
line. Criteria that cannot be observed without a running server are not in this
document; everything here is testable offline with a stub client and a
`mkdtempSync` state directory.

**Terminology.** A *slot* is one entry in `presets/free-tier.json`, carrying a model and a `weight`. A slot's `weight` is its active-session budget for one pass: the number of concurrent claims it may hold before the next slot is preferred. A *pass* is one declaration-order sweep of the slot list; the pool runs one pass, and a slot's cap is its weight. There is no slot cap, and a model may appear on more than one line — each line is its own slot with its own weight. Preference is by declaration order, never by weight. A *base* is a pooled agent type (`explore`), and its slot holders are `<base>-<slot>`, hidden in `opencode.jsonc`. A *claim* is a running spawn recorded in `claims.<pid>.json`. A *context map* is the five-file `.opencode/context/` codemap described in Epic G.

---

## Epics and the pains behind them

| Epic | Pain point it solves |
| --- | --- |
| **A — Cost control** | Quota exhaustion. Routine work (grep, reading, cartography) consumes the same expensive budget as design work, and the main model is spent on file listing. |
| **B — Provider resilience** | Provider limits. Free-tier quotas are per-provider and per-minute, so a long session hard-fails the moment one provider's window closes, even while three other providers sit idle. |
| **C — Hang recovery** | Hangs. A wedged or silently-stalled subagent holds its slot forever; one bad task stalls the session with no error and no timeout. |
| **D — Notifications** | Parallel sessions. With several sessions open, work finishing — or a question blocking — is invisible unless you happen to be looking at that terminal. |
| **E — Remote hosts** | Remote SSH notification. Work runs on remote hosts, so notifications raised there die on that host's nonexistent desktop instead of reaching the local one. |
| **F — Adoption and safety** | Installability. A personal config cannot be adopted safely: it either clobbers what you already have, or needs manual surgery before it runs. |
| **G — Context and cost** | Cold exploration. Every task starts by re-discovering the structure of the codebase from scratch, so the same layout is re-read — and re-paid for — on every single run. |
| **K — Autonomy modes** | Stalls. A long run stops for every routine permission, or waits for a human to answer a question the agent could decide itself, even when its own recommendation is clear. |

---

## Epic A — Cost control (route bulk work off the expensive model)

### US-1: Bulk exploration runs on cheap/free subagents
**As an** opencode user paying per token, **I want** file reading and searching delegated to cheap subagents, **so that** my main model's budget goes to design work instead of grep.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-1
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given the root agent `build` with read/glob/grep denied, When a read-family tool is invoked, Then the call is denied and the agent is pointed at an exploration base rather than executing inline.
- [ ] Given a pooled base such as `explore` is spawned, When the plugin rewrites the spawn, Then the concrete model selected is a slot declared in `presets/free-tier.json`.
- [ ] Given a pool whose slots are all zero-cost, When N exploration spawns run, Then none of them is dispatched to a paid model.

### US-2: One knob selects the exploration/implementation model
**As a** user, **I want** to change which model handles delegated work without editing prompts, **so that** I can change cost strategy in one place.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-2
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given the pool preset is edited to swap a slot's model, When a pooled spawn is routed, Then the new model is used with no change to any agent prompt in `opencode.jsonc`.
- [ ] Given `opencode.jsonc` hard-codes a model for a pooled agent, When the plugin boots, Then it warns that the hard-coded value is overridden and that `presets/free-tier.json` wins.
- [ ] Given a slot declares an invalid `weight`, When the pool loads, Then it falls back to weight 1 and warns, rather than dropping the slot.

### US-3: Reproducible cost benchmark
**As a** maintainer, **I want** a script that measures the token/cost of a representative task with and without the pool, **so that** any savings claim is measured rather than asserted.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-3
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given the benchmark script is run against a fixed task prompt, When it executes, Then it reports token counts and cost for the pooled run and the unpooled run from the same input.
- [ ] Given a slot's model is free, When the benchmark prices it, Then its cost is 0 rather than unknown or omitted.
- [ ] Given the benchmark runs with no network access, When it cannot reach a pricing source, Then it fails loudly instead of reporting 0 cost for a paid model.

### US-23: The pool takes any model; free is the shipped default, not an enforced rule
**As a** user, **I want** the pool to accept whatever models I give it and only default to free ones, **so that** I keep full control of what the pool runs on instead of being second-guessed about it.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-23

This is the policy behind US-1 and it does not contradict US-7. The pool exists to take **mechanical** work — reading, searching, mechanical edits, cartography — off the main model, so the bundled preset ships free models: that is what those tokens cost when you have not said otherwise. It is a **default, not a restriction**. LaCode holds no opinion about which models a user may run: no whitelist, no filter, no per-model rule beyond the structural `provider/model-id` shape a slot must have to be addressable at all. There is no cost advisory either — a plugin that guesses what a model costs from a pinned snapshot it does not ship would be advisory theatre, so the shipped default is expressed once, in `presets/free-tier.json`, where a user reads it and edits it.

The reconciliation with US-7 is that **acceptance and endorsement are different claims**: the pool accepts anything, and the preset states what it is for.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given the bundled preset, When its slots are priced against the pinned models.dev snapshot, Then every slot is free or very cheap, and any slot the snapshot cannot price is named as unknown rather than assumed to be free.
- [ ] Given a pool configured with any arbitrary `provider/model-id` string — a paid one, an exotic one, an invented one — When the plugin boots and a spawn is routed, Then the model binds verbatim and runs, with no warning about it, no rejection of it, and no special-casing of it.
- [ ] Given the shipped preset, When a user reads it, Then it says the pool is for mechanical work, and says they MAY substitute their own list via `~/.config/lacode/pool.json`, so the free default never reads as a prohibition.
- [ ] Given no price information exists for a configured model, When the plugin boots, Then it is silent: the pool does not inspect, fetch, or infer prices at all, because a default is expressed in the preset and not enforced at runtime.
- [ ] Given a paid or exotic model is configured in the pool, When a spawn is routed, Then it is routed to that model exactly as any other slot would be, because rejecting it would break US-7.

---

## Epic B — Provider resilience (weighted model pool)

### US-4: Automatic failover when a provider rate-limits
**As a** user on free tiers that hit per-provider limits, **I want** subagents to move to a different provider automatically, **so that** long sessions do not fail.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-4
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given a spawn fails with a rate-limit-shaped error, When the error is serialized and matched, Then the offending model is marked cooling and a cooldown file is written for it.
- [ ] Given model A is cooling and another slot is usable, When the next spawn is routed, Then the pick is a different usable model, never the cooling one.
- [ ] Given a pooled task completes with an empty result, When the task hook returns, Then that model is benched for `empty response`, the result explains the bench, and the next spawn routes to another slot.
- [ ] Given two distinct models on one provider fail with transient, non-quota errors inside ten minutes, When the second failure is recorded, Then every slot on that provider is benched for one flat `provider-degraded` window and the next spawn routes to another provider.
- [ ] Given a provider-degraded window lapses, When a probe answers on one of its models, Then that model is re-admitted without a restart, because the bench was evidence about the provider, not a strike against the model.
- [ ] Given every model is cooling, When a spawn is routed, Then the spawn is refused explicitly with a message naming the cooling slots and their reasons, and no model is routed to.
- [ ] Given a limit error names a reset time, When the cooldown is recorded, Then the stated reset is used instead of a guessed backoff.

### US-5: Slots fill in declaration order in one pass, with repeats
**As a** user, **I want** work to prefer the first slot and spill to later slots only when the earlier ones are full, **so that** a healthy preferred model is used before fallbacks and no slot is used while an earlier usable slot has room.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-5
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given live claims, When the pool has room, Then the lowest-index usable slot whose load is below its weight is chosen, and a slot declared later is not used until every earlier usable slot has reached its weight.
- [ ] Given a model appears on more than one line, When the pool loads, Then each line is its own slot with its own weight, and the later line adds seats at its own position.
- [ ] Given a slot is cooling or unavailable, When its position comes up, Then it is skipped and the pass continues to the next slot.
- [ ] Given a claim is released, When the next spawn is routed, Then the slot that freed capacity is preferred again in declaration order; no stored position keeps it waiting.
- [ ] Given every usable slot is at its weight, When another spawn is routed, Then it goes to the least-loaded usable slot as overflow, and the pool never refuses work while at least one slot is usable.
- [ ] Given all slots carry equal weight, When spawns are routed, Then the same ordered one-pass fill applies.
- [ ] Given per-slot load is read, When it is asserted, Then a slot's load never exceeds its weight except through overflow.

### US-6: Live pool visibility
**As a** user, **I want** to see per-slot load and which model is cooling and why, **so that** I understand where my subagents are going.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-6
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given claims are held by several processes, When the status view is requested, Then it shows every process's claims and the aggregate load per slot.
- [ ] Given a model is cooling with a stated reason, When the status view is requested, Then the model is listed as cooling together with that reason.
- [ ] Given a claim file is older than the dead-file threshold, When the status view is computed, Then the stale claim is pruned rather than counted.
- [ ] Given a slot is at its weight, When the status view is requested, Then it is not marked as the slot the next spawn would take while any usable slot is below its weight; when every usable slot is at its weight, the least-loaded slot is marked next.
- [ ] Given the pool is filling, When the status view is requested, Then it shows whether the next spawn is a normal pick or overflow.

### US-7: Non-free models still work
**As a** user who wants a paid model in the pool, **I want** to supply any model list, **so that** the pool is not restricted to free tiers.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-7
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given a slot names a paid model, When the pool loads, Then the slot is accepted and routed to without a free-tier filter rejecting it.
- [ ] Given a model id contains a vendor prefix with slashes (e.g. `openrouter/nvidia/model:free`), When it is split into provider and model id, Then the split is on the first slash only and the id tail is preserved.
- [ ] Given a pool file declares more slots than the built-in warning threshold, When the pool loads, Then every entry is kept and a warning names the count; there is no slot cap.
- [ ] Given a provider configured with **no** `whitelist` key, When the config hook binds a slot on that provider, Then no `whitelist` is written for it, because an absent whitelist already allows every model the provider offers.
- [ ] Given a provider the pool never names a slot on, When the config hook runs, Then that provider entry is left exactly as it was, with no `whitelist` key added.
- [ ] Given a provider that already carries a `whitelist`, When the config hook binds a slot model on it, Then the model id is appended and every entry the user wrote is preserved in order.
- [ ] Given any provider after the config hook has run, When its whitelist is inspected, Then it is either absent or non-empty, because an empty allowlist names no model at all and opencode deletes the provider outright.

`provider.<name>.whitelist` is an **allowlist**, not a to-do list: opencode
deletes every model a provider offers that the whitelist does not name, and
deletes the provider itself if nothing survives. An absent whitelist is the open
form — everything is allowed. That makes writing one where the user had none the
single most destructive thing the plugin could do, since a list holding only the
pool's models silently deletes everything else they run there. So appending is
correct exactly when a whitelist exists (it is a real restriction, and the pool
models would otherwise resolve to nothing) and is not merely unnecessary when one
does not.

### US-28: A local gateway (OmniRoute) is registered as an ordinary provider
**As a** user running a local OpenAI-compatible gateway, **I want** LaCode to register it so its models are selectable and I can name one in my pool, **so that** *I* decide whether pooled work drains through it instead of the bundled models.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-28
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given `omniroute.enabled` with a reachable gateway, When the config hook runs, Then LaCode registers a `provider.omniroute` entry exposing the gateway's models (everything it lists, or filtered by `models`/`combo`), and writes NOTHING into the pool.

## Epic K — Autonomy modes (YOLO and YKB)

### US-37: YOLO mode approves permissions without stopping
**As a** user running a long autonomous task, **I want** permission prompts to be approved automatically while YOLO is on, **so that** the agent keeps working instead of waiting for routine approvals, while an explicit `deny` still protects me.

Permission prompts are the main thing that breaks a long autonomous run: every `ask` blocks the session until a human answers. YOLO flips that decision to `allow` at the permission hook, keeps an explicit `deny` authoritative, and answers any request that still reaches the event bus. The state lives in the `yolo` option on the lacode plugin entry in the global `opencode.jsonc`; the TUI writes it and the server reads it on the next decision, so enabling it also clears what is already pending.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-37
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given YOLO is on, When the runtime's permission decision is `ask`, Then it becomes `allow` without a prompt, while an existing `deny` or `allow` is left unchanged.
- [ ] Given YOLO is off, When the runtime's permission decision is `ask`, Then it stays `ask` and still reaches the user.
- [ ] Given a `permission.asked` event still reaches the event bus while YOLO is on and carries a request id and a session id, When the handler runs, Then the plugin replies `once` for that request; an event missing either id is ignored.
- [ ] Given YOLO is toggled in the TUI, When the global `opencode.jsonc` changes, Then the next permission decision sees the new value without a restart, and requests already pending are answered.
- [ ] Given the TUI toggles a mode, When it writes the global `opencode.jsonc`, Then only the `yolo` / `ykb` options on the lacode plugin entry change, comments and formatting are preserved, and the config remains the single source of truth.
- [ ] Given the README and configuration reference, Then the `yolo` option and the `/yolo` command are documented alongside `/modes`.

### US-38: YKB mode chooses the recommendation instead of asking
**As a** user who wants the agent to keep moving, **I want** YKB (You Know Better) mode to suppress questions and pick the recommended option itself, **so that** it finishes or blocks on a real dependency rather than waiting for me to choose.

A question costs a full turn and a human decision, even when the agent has a clear recommendation. YKB adds a system instruction that tells the agent to choose and continue, and auto-answers any question that still reaches the runtime with its `(Recommended)` option (or the first option when none is marked). A free-text question with no options is left for the user, because there is nothing to choose.

**Story ID(s) for tests:** US-38
**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] Given YKB is on, When a request is built, Then the system prompt carries the YKB instruction exactly once; when YKB is off, the instruction is absent.
- [ ] Given a question offers options and YKB is on, When the plugin answers it, Then each question selects the option marked `(Recommended)` (case-insensitive, in the label or description), or the first option when none is marked.
- [ ] Given a question has no options, When YKB sees it, Then it leaves the question for the user and records a warning rather than inventing an answer.
- [ ] Given YKB is off, When a question is asked, Then the plugin sends no answer.
- [ ] Given YKB is toggled on in the TUI, When questions are already pending, Then they are answered with the same recommendation rule.
- [ ] Given YOLO and YKB are both on, When permission and question events arrive, Then each mode acts only on its own event and the other mode's behavior is unchanged.
- [ ] Given the README and configuration reference, Then the `ykb` option and the `/ykb` and `/modes` commands are documented.
